text: How do antiseptics differ from disinfectants? State the role of the following chemicals in the food industry: (i) Sodium benzoate (ii) Aspartame
modelAnswer:
Antiseptics are chemicals that kill or inhibit growth of microorganisms and are safe enough to be applied on living tissues (e.g., skin, wounds), such as dilute iodine tincture. Disinfectants also kill microorganisms but are too harsh to be applied to living tissue — they are used on inanimate objects/surfaces (e.g., floors, instruments), such as 1% phenol solution. The same chemical can act as an antiseptic in dilute form and a disinfectant in concentrated form.
(i) Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative — it prevents growth of bacteria, yeast and mould in acidic foods.
(ii) Aspartame is used as an artificial (low-calorie) sweetening agent in food and beverages.
keyPoints: Antiseptics: safe on living tissue; Disinfectants: used on non-living surfaces

text: The freezing point of a solution containing 5.85g of NaCl in 100g of water is −3.348°C. Calculate van't Hoff factor 'i' for this solution. What will be the experimental molecular weight of NaCl? (Kf for water = 1.86 K kg mol-1, at. wt. Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)

Theoretical ΔTf = Kf × m = 1.86 × 1.0 = 1.86 K.
Observed ΔTf = 3.348 K.

Experimental molecular weight = Theoretical mol. wt./i = 58.5/1.8 = 32.5 g/mol.

text: Give reason for each of the following: (a) For ferric hydroxide sol the coagulating power of phosphate ion is more than chloride ion. (b) Medicines are more effective in their colloidal form. (c) Gelatin is added to ice creams.
modelAnswer:
(a) Ferric hydroxide sol is positively charged, so it is coagulated by anions. According to the Hardy-Schulze rule, the coagulating power of an ion increases with its charge. Phosphate ion (PO4³⁻) has a higher (−3) charge than chloride ion (Cl⁻, −1 charge), so phosphate has much greater coagulating power.
(b) Colloidal particles have an extremely large surface area to volume ratio, which increases their solubility, absorption and reactivity in the body, making medicines in colloidal form more easily and effectively absorbed/assimilated.
(c) Gelatin is a protective colloid that is added to ice cream to prevent the coalescence/crystallisation of ice and fat particles, giving the ice cream a smooth texture and preventing it from separating into a coarse, grainy mass.
keyPoints: Hardy-Schulze rule: higher ionic charge → greater coagulating power (PO4³⁻ > Cl⁻)
Colloidal medicines: large surface area → better absorption
Gelatin: protective colloid, prevents ice-crystal growth in ice cream

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain why: (i) Mn2+ is more stable than Fe2+ towards oxidation to +3 state. (At. no. of Mn = 25, Fe = 26) (ii) Transition elements usually form coloured ions. (iii) Zr and Hf exhibit similar properties. (At. no. of Zr = 40, Hf = 72)
modelAnswer:
(i) Mn2+ has configuration [Ar]3d5, which is a stable half-filled d-subshell (extra stability due to symmetrical distribution and exchange energy). Oxidising Mn2+ to Mn3+ (3d4) would disturb this stable half-filled configuration, making it unfavourable. Fe2+ ([Ar]3d6) readily loses one electron to attain the more stable half-filled Fe3+ (3d5) configuration. Hence Mn2+ resists oxidation more than Fe2+.
(ii) Transition metal ions usually have partially filled d-orbitals. In the presence of ligands, the degenerate d-orbitals split into two sets of different energies (crystal field splitting). Electrons can undergo d-d transitions by absorbing light of a specific wavelength from the visible region to jump between these split levels; the complementary wavelength is transmitted/reflected, giving the ion its observed colour.
(iii) Zr (Z=40, 4d series) and Hf (Z=72, 5d series) belong to the same group. Due to the lanthanide contraction (the steady decrease in atomic/ionic radii across the lanthanides between La and Hf), the atomic and ionic radii of Hf become almost identical to those of Zr, despite the large difference in atomic number. This results in very similar chemical properties for the two elements.
keyPoints: Mn2+ (3d5, half-filled) resists further oxidation, unlike Fe2+ (3d6→3d5 favourable)
Coloured ions: d-d electronic transitions due to crystal field splitting
Zr & Hf similar due to lanthanide contraction equalising their radii

subject: Chemistry
text: Name the sulphide ore of Copper. Describe how pure copper is extracted from this ore.
modelAnswer:
The sulphide ore of copper is Copper pyrites (Chalcopyrite), CuFeS2.
Extraction: The crushed and concentrated ore (by froth flotation) is roasted in air to remove volatile impurities and convert some sulphide to oxide. The roasted ore is then smelted with silica (SiO2) and coke in a reverberatory/blast furnace; FeO reacts with SiO2 to form a slag (FeSiO3) that is removed, leaving behind a molten mixture of Cu2S and FeS called copper matte.
The matte is charged into a Bessemer converter with silica and blown with air; the remaining FeS is oxidised and removed as slag, and Cu2S is partially oxidised to Cu2O. The Cu2S and Cu2O react (self-reduction/auto-reduction): Cu2S + 2Cu2O → 6Cu + SO2. This gives blister copper (~98% pure).
Blister copper is finally purified by electrolytic refining: impure copper as anode, pure copper strip as cathode, in CuSO4/H2SO4 electrolyte; pure Cu deposits at the cathode while impurities fall as anode mud.
keyPoints: Roasting → smelting (with SiO2, coke) → copper matte (Cu2S+FeS)

subject: Chemistry
text: Calculate the emf and ΔG for the cell reaction at 25°C: Zn(s) | Zn2+(0.1M) || Cd2+(0.01M) | Cd(s). Given E°(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.763V and E°(Cd2+/Cd) = −0.403V. Also define: (1) Equivalent conductivity (2) Corrosion of metals.
modelAnswer:
Cell reaction: Zn(s) + Cd2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cd(s); n = 2.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = E°(Cd2+/Cd) − E°(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.403 − (−0.763) = +0.360 V.
Using Nernst equation at 25°C:
Ecell = E°cell − (0.0591/n) log([Zn2+]/[Cd2+]) = 0.360 − (0.0591/2) log(0.1/0.01)
= 0.360 − 0.02955 × log(10) = 0.360 − 0.02955 = 0.3305 V.
ΔG = −nFEcell = −2 × 96500 × 0.3305 = −63,787 J/mol ≈ −63.79 kJ/mol.
(1) Equivalent conductivity: the conducting power of all the ions produced by one gram equivalent of an electrolyte dissolved in a given volume of solution.
(2) Corrosion of metals: the spontaneous electrochemical process by which a metal is gradually oxidised/degraded on exposure to atmospheric conditions (oxygen, moisture), e.g. formation of rust (Fe2O3.xH2O) on iron.

subject: Chemistry
text: The specific conductivity of a solution containing 5g of anhydrous BaCl2 (mol. wt. = 208) in 1000 cm3 of a solution is found to be 0.0058 ohm-1cm-1. Calculate the molar and equivalent conductivity of the solution. What is an electrochemical series? How is it useful in predicting whether a metal can liberate hydrogen from acid or not?
modelAnswer:
Molarity C = (5/208) mol in 1000 cm3 = 0.02404 mol/L = 0.02404×10⁻3 mol/cm3.
Molar conductivity Λm = κ×1000/C(mol/L) = 0.0058×1000/0.02404 = 241.3 ohm⁻1cm2mol⁻1.
BaCl2 has equivalent weight = 208/2 = 104, so normality N = 5/104×1 = 0.0481 eq/L.
Equivalent conductivity Λeq = κ×1000/N = 0.0058×1000/0.0481 = 120.6 ohm⁻1cm2eq⁻1.

An electrochemical series (activity series) is the arrangement of metals (and hydrogen) in order of their decreasing standard reduction potentials (or increasing standard oxidation potentials/reactivity). A metal placed above hydrogen in this series (i.e., with a more negative/lower reduction potential than hydrogen, E° < 0) can displace/liberate hydrogen gas from dilute acids, since it is a stronger reducing agent than hydrogen and gets oxidised while H+ is reduced to H2. Metals placed below hydrogen (E° > 0, e.g. Cu, Ag) cannot liberate hydrogen from acids.
keyPoints: Molar conductivity Λm ≈ 241.3 ohm⁻1 cm2 mol⁻1
Equivalent conductivity Λeq ≈ 120.6 ohm⁻1 cm2 eq⁻1
Electrochemical series: metals ranked by E°; those above H2 (E°<0) liberate H2 from acids

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain why: (1) Nitrogen does not form pentahalides. (2) Helium is used for filling weather balloons. (3) ICl is more reactive than I2. Draw the structures of the following: (1) HClO4 (2) H3PO3
modelAnswer:
(1) Nitrogen (Z=7) has no d-orbitals in its valence shell (n=2), so it cannot expand its octet to accommodate 5 bond pairs; hence it cannot form pentahalides like NCl5 (it forms only trihalides, NX3). Heavier group 15 elements like P, As, Sb have accessible d-orbitals and do form pentahalides (PCl5, etc.).
(2) Helium is extremely light (low density), chemically inert (non-flammable, unlike hydrogen) and non-toxic, making it safe for filling weather/observation balloons that must rise through the atmosphere without risk of explosion.
(3) ICl (interhalogen compound) has a weaker I–Cl bond than the I–I bond in I2 because the two atoms are dissimilar (bond is polar, and interhalogen bonds are generally weaker/more reactive than the corresponding X–X bonds); this makes ICl more reactive as a halogenating agent than I2.

(1) HClO4 (perchloric acid) structure: central Cl atom tetrahedrally bonded to four oxygen atoms — three as Cl=O (double bonds) and one as Cl–O–H.
(2) H3PO3 (phosphorous acid) structure: central P atom bonded to one P=O (double bond), two P–OH groups, and one P–H bond directly (tetrahedral geometry around P); it is dibasic despite having 3 hydrogens because one H is directly bonded to P (non-ionisable).
keyPoints: N has no d-orbitals → cannot expand octet → no NCl5
He: light, inert, non-flammable → used in weather balloons
ICl more reactive than I2 due to polar/weaker interhalogen bond
HClO4: Cl bonded to 3=O and 1 OH tetrahedrally
H3PO3: P bonded to =O, 2 OH, 1 P-H directly (dibasic)

text: (Alternative to Q17) Explain why: (1) Mercury loses its meniscus in contact with ozone. (2) Halogens are coloured and the colour deepens on moving down the group from fluorine to iodine. (3) Hydride of sulphur is a gas while hydride of oxygen is a liquid. Complete and balance: (1) NaCl + MnO2 + H2SO4 → (2) KMnO4 + SO2 + H2O →
modelAnswer:
(1) Ozone oxidises mercury, forming a thin film of mercurous oxide on its surface; this film sticks to glass, causing mercury to lose its characteristic convex meniscus and wet the glass surface (tailing of mercury).
(2) Halogens absorb visible light causing electronic transitions (excitation of electrons from HOMO to LUMO); as we move down the group (F→Cl→Br→I), the HOMO-LUMO energy gap decreases (due to increasing atomic size/decreasing ionisation energy), so the wavelength of light absorbed increases and shifts toward the red/lower energy end, making the colour progressively deeper.
(3) Oxygen forms strong hydrogen bonds between H2O molecules (O is highly electronegative and small), giving water a high boiling point and making it liquid at room temperature. Sulphur, being larger and less electronegative, does not form significant hydrogen bonds in H2S; H2S has only weak van der Waals forces between molecules, so it has a low boiling point and remains a gas at room temperature.

(1) 2NaCl + MnO2 + 3H2SO4 → 2NaHSO4 + MnSO4 + Cl2 + 2H2O
(2) 2KMnO4 + 5SO2 + 2H2O → K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 2H2SO4

text: (Alternative to Q18) Write chemical equations to illustrate the following name reactions: (1) Clemmensen's reduction (2) Rosenmund's reduction (3) HVZ reaction. Explain why: (1) Acetaldehyde undergoes aldol condensation, but formaldehyde does not. (2) Acetic acid is a weaker acid as compared to formic acid.
modelAnswer:
(1) Clemmensen's reduction: a ketone/aldehyde is reduced to the corresponding alkane using zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl:
CH3COCH3 + 4[H] →(Zn-Hg/conc.HCl)→ CH3CH2CH3 + H2O
(2) Rosenmund's reduction: an acid chloride is selectively reduced to an aldehyde using H2 gas over a Pd catalyst poisoned with BaSO4 (to prevent over-reduction to alcohol):
CH3COCl + H2 →(Pd/BaSO4)→ CH3CHO + HCl
(3) HVZ (Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky) reaction: carboxylic acids with an α-hydrogen react with Cl2/Br2 in presence of red phosphorus to give α-halo carboxylic acids:
CH3COOH + Br2 →(red P)→ CH2BrCOOH + HBr

(1) Acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) has an α-hydrogen (on the methyl group) which can be removed by a base to form a carbanion/enolate that attacks another aldehyde molecule's carbonyl carbon, giving aldol condensation. Formaldehyde (HCHO) has no α-carbon/α-hydrogen (the carbonyl carbon is bonded only to H atoms), so it cannot undergo aldol condensation; instead it undergoes Cannizzaro reaction.
(2) In formic acid (HCOOH), the H atom directly attached to the carbonyl carbon has essentially no electron-donating effect, so the O-H bond is more polarised and ionises more readily. In acetic acid (CH3COOH), the electron-donating (+I) methyl group pushes electron density onto the carboxylate, destabilising the conjugate base (acetate ion) relative to formate, and making the O-H less polar/less easily ionised. Hence formic acid is a stronger acid than acetic acid (acetic acid is weaker).
keyPoints: Formaldehyde has no α-H → no aldol condensation
CH3 +I effect in acetic acid destabilises conjugate base → weaker acid than HCOOH

text: Explain why: (i) Transition elements form alloys. (ii) Zn2+ salts are white whereas Cu2+ salts are coloured. (iii) Transition metals and their compounds act as catalyst.

(ii) Zn2+ has configuration [Ar]3d10 — a completely filled d-subshell, so no d-d electronic transitions are possible, hence Zn2+ salts are white/colourless. Cu2+ has configuration [Ar]3d9 — a partially filled d-subshell, allowing d-d electronic transitions upon absorption of visible light, giving Cu2+ salts their characteristic blue colour.
(iii) Transition metals and their compounds can adopt variable oxidation states and have vacant d-orbitals available to form temporary/intermediate bonds with reactant molecules (providing an alternate lower-activation-energy pathway), and can also provide a large surface area for adsorption of reactants (heterogeneous catalysis). This makes them effective catalysts, e.g. Fe in the Haber process, V2O5 in the Contact process.

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain why: (1) Fluorine has lower electron affinity than chlorine. (2) Red phosphorus is less reactive than white phosphorous. (3) Ozone acts as a powerful oxidising agent. Draw the structures of the following: (1) XeF6 (2) IF7
modelAnswer:
(1) Fluorine has a very small atomic size, so its 2p orbitals experience significant inter-electronic repulsion when an extra electron is added, which partially offsets the favourable energy release; this makes fluorine's electron affinity lower than that of chlorine, which has a larger 3p subshell with less electron-electron repulsion.
(2) White phosphorus has a strained tetrahedral P4 structure with P-P-P bond angles of 60°, causing considerable angular/ring strain and making it highly reactive. Red phosphorus has a polymeric chain structure (formed by linking P4 units) with no such strain, making it thermodynamically more stable and much less reactive than white phosphorus.
(3) Ozone readily decomposes to give O2 and a nascent (highly reactive) oxygen atom [O3 → O2 + [O]], which is a powerful oxidising species due to its high electronegativity and tendency to gain electrons, making ozone a powerful oxidising agent.

(1) XeF6: distorted octahedral (pentagonal bipyramidal-derived) structure — Xe with 6 bond pairs + 1 lone pair, sp3d3 hybridisation.
(2) IF7: pentagonal bipyramidal structure — I with 7 bond pairs, sp3d3 hybridisation.
keyPoints: F has lower EA than Cl due to small size/high electron-electron repulsion in 2p
White P (strained P4, 60° angles) more reactive than red P (polymeric, unstrained)
O3 → O2 + [O] (nascent oxygen) makes ozone a strong oxidiser

text: State reasons for the following: (i) Ethylamine is soluble in water whereas aniline is insoluble in water. (ii) Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than aromatic amines.
modelAnswer:
(i) Ethylamine (a small aliphatic amine) can form hydrogen bonds effectively with water molecules through its -NH2 group and has a small hydrophobic ethyl group, making it soluble in water. Aniline has a large hydrophobic phenyl ring that dominates its overall polarity, and its lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the ring (reducing its ability to hydrogen-bond as effectively), making aniline poorly soluble/insoluble in water.
(ii) In aliphatic amines, the alkyl group has a +I (electron-donating) effect that increases electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more available for protonation (more basic). In aromatic amines like aniline, the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised (conjugated) into the benzene ring, reducing its availability for protonation, making aromatic amines much weaker bases than aliphatic amines.
keyPoints: Ethylamine: small size, H-bonds with water → soluble

Aromatic amines: lone pair delocalised into ring → less basic

text: Explain what is observed when: (i) A beam of light is passed through a colloidal solution. (ii) An electric current is passed through a colloidal solution. (iii) An electrolyte (AlCl3) is added to a colloidal solution of arsenious sulphide (As2S3).
modelAnswer:
(i) When a beam of light is passed through a colloidal solution, the path of light becomes visible when viewed at right angles due to scattering of light by the colloidal particles; this phenomenon is called the Tyndall effect.
(ii) When an electric current is passed through a colloidal solution, the charged colloidal particles migrate towards the oppositely charged electrode (electrophoresis); e.g., negatively charged As2S3 sol particles move towards the anode.
(iii) AlCl3 is an electrolyte that furnishes Al3+ ions. Since As2S3 sol is negatively charged, the Al3+ (trivalent cation) is highly effective at neutralising the charge on the colloidal particles (Hardy-Schulze rule: higher charge = greater coagulating power), causing the particles to lose their stability and coagulate/precipitate out of the sol.
keyPoints: Light scattering by colloid particles = Tyndall effect

text: Explain the following: (i) Transition metals and their compounds generally exhibit a paramagnetic behaviour. (ii) There is an increase in density of elements from titanium (Z=22) to copper (Z=29) in the 3d series of transition elements. (iii) K2Cr2O7 acts as a powerful oxidising agent in acidic medium.
modelAnswer:
(i) Transition metals and their compounds generally have partially filled (n-1)d orbitals with unpaired electrons; unpaired electrons give rise to a net magnetic moment, making these species paramagnetic.
(ii) Across the 3d series from Ti to Cu, atomic mass increases substantially while atomic (metallic) radius decreases only slightly/stays nearly constant (due to poor shielding by d-electrons balancing the increasing nuclear charge). Since density = mass/volume, the increasing mass combined with nearly constant volume causes density to increase progressively from Ti to Cu.
(iii) In acidic medium, dichromate ion (Cr2O7²⁻) is readily reduced, with Cr going from +6 to +3 oxidation state, gaining a large number of electrons per formula unit (Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H+ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O), and has a high standard reduction potential (E° = +1.33V) in acidic medium, making it a powerful oxidising agent under these conditions.

Density increases Ti→Cu: mass increases faster than radius decreases

Δp = p°×(m×18/1000) = 23.756×(0.3226×18/1000) = 23.756×0.005807 = 0.1379 mm Hg.

text: State one reason for each of the following: (i) Alkylamine is soluble in water whereas arylamine is insoluble in water. (ii) Methylamine is a stronger base than methyl alcohol.
modelAnswer:
(i) Alkylamines (small aliphatic amines) can form strong hydrogen bonds with water through the -NH2 group and have small hydrophobic alkyl chains, making them soluble in water. Arylamines have a bulky hydrophobic aromatic ring, and the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the ring, reducing effective hydrogen bonding with water, making them poorly soluble/insoluble in water.
(ii) In methylamine (CH3NH2), the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen is localised and readily available for donation/protonation, and the +I effect of the methyl group further increases electron density on N. In methanol (CH3OH), the lone pair on the more electronegative oxygen is held more tightly and less available for donation. Hence methylamine, with its more available/basic lone pair on nitrogen, is a much stronger base than methyl alcohol.
keyPoints: Alkylamine: H-bonds with water, small alkyl group → soluble; Arylamine: bulky ring, delocalised lone pair → insoluble

text: State a reason for each of the following: (i) La(OH)3 is more basic than Lu(OH)3. (ii) Transition elements and their compounds act as catalyst.
modelAnswer:
(i) Across the lanthanide series, ionic radius decreases steadily from La3+ to Lu3+ due to lanthanide contraction. A smaller cation holds the OH⁻ ion more tightly/covalently (less ionic character), reducing the basicity of the hydroxide. Since La3+ is the largest lanthanide ion, La(OH)3 is more ionic and hence more basic than Lu(OH)3, whose smaller Lu3+ ion makes the hydroxide comparatively less basic (more covalent character).
(ii) Transition elements exhibit variable oxidation states and have vacant d-orbitals available to form unstable/intermediate complexes with reactant molecules, providing an alternate reaction pathway of lower activation energy; they can also adsorb reactants on their surface (large surface area), increasing reaction rate. These properties make transition metals and their compounds effective catalysts.
keyPoints: Lanthanide contraction: La3+ (largest) → most basic hydroxide; Lu3+ (smallest) → least basic
Transition metals: variable oxidation states + vacant d-orbitals + adsorption → catalytic activity

subject: Chemistry
text: Account for the following: (i) Phenol is a stronger acid than aliphatic alcohols. (ii) Ethanol gives iodoform reaction whereas methanol does not give iodoform reaction. (iii) Ethers should not be distilled to dryness.
modelAnswer:
(i) In phenol, the -OH group is attached directly to the aromatic ring; the lone pair on oxygen is delocalised (conjugated) into the ring, which withdraws electron density from O and stabilises the phenoxide ion (conjugate base) formed after loss of H+ through resonance. Aliphatic alcohols have no such resonance stabilisation of their alkoxide ion, and the alkyl group's +I effect further destabilises the alkoxide. Hence phenol ionises more readily and is a stronger acid than aliphatic alcohols.
(ii) The iodoform reaction requires a CH3-CH(OH)- group (or CH3CO- group). Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) has this CH3-CH(OH)- structural feature and gives a positive iodoform test (forms CHI3 yellow ppt). Methanol (CH3OH) does not have a CH3-CH(OH)- group (it is CH2(OH)- essentially with only one carbon), so it does not give the iodoform reaction.
(iii) Ethers (e.g., diethyl ether) slowly form explosive peroxides on prolonged exposure to air/light. These peroxides have a higher boiling point than the ether itself and remain behind as the ether is distilled off; as distillation continues to dryness, the concentration of the peroxide residue increases and can explode due to the heat of distillation. Hence ethers should never be distilled to complete dryness.
keyPoints: Phenol: resonance-stabilised phenoxide ion → stronger acid than alcohols
Iodoform test needs CH3CH(OH)- group: ethanol has it, methanol doesn't
Ethers form explosive peroxides on standing; distilling to dryness concentrates and can detonate them

If the conductivity of 0.1M KCl solution is 0.0129 ohm-1cm-1, calculate the cell constant and molar conductivity of 0.02M NaCl solution. The emf (E°cell) of the following reaction is 0.89V: 3Sn4+ + 2Cr → 3Sn2+ + 2Cr3+. Calculate the value of ΔG° for the reaction. Predict whether the above reaction will be spontaneous or not.
modelAnswer:
Cell constant G* = κ(KCl)×R(KCl) = 0.0129×200 = 2.58 cm⁻1.
Conductivity of NaCl solution κ(NaCl) = G*/R(NaCl) = 2.58/1100 = 2.345×10⁻3 ohm⁻1cm⁻1.
Molar conductivity of NaCl = κ×1000/C = (2.345×10⁻3×1000)/0.02 = 117.3 ohm⁻1cm2mol⁻1.

For the reaction 3Sn4+ + 2Cr → 3Sn2+ + 2Cr3+, n = 6 (2 Cr atoms each lose 3 electrons = 6 electrons transferred).
ΔG° = −nFE°cell = −6×96500×0.89 = −515,310 J/mol ≈ −515.31 kJ/mol.
Since ΔG° is negative, the reaction is spontaneous.
